title: Teach confusable pairs explicitly
statement: Teach confusable ideas as a pair: start with clear-cut examples that tell them apart, keep borderline cases for later, contrast them explicitly, and mix them only once both are learned.
example: One reading course's knowledge graph had 1 confusable link among 47 components.
detail: The reading project's alignment plan types discriminations as gateway hard prerequisites and records that they are chronically under-modelled: its Grade 5 graph had 1 confusable edge among 47 knowledge components (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/docs/academics-alignment-plan.md`). The generic instruction BrainLift says students don't reliably discover discriminations alone, so the contrast is taught explicitly with near-miss pairs (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Generic Instruction BrainLift.md`), and the curriculum BrainLift says the graph should encode confusable pairs, since interleaving after both are learned builds discrimination (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/feedback/feedback1/Curriculum & Knowledge BrainLift.md`). Record each pair, choose those first examples so the confusion doesn't form, and teach the contrast side by side (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0116-graph-architecture-brainlift-core.qmd`).
against: Interleaving helps mainly where telling the two apart is part of the learning problem (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/knowledge/kb-0119-curriculum-architecture-brainlift-evidence.qmd`). The course graph is a draft awaiting academic review (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/applied/g3-course-graph.qmd`).
